This paper explores the performance of randomly constructed low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes with degree distributions related to degree two, across a binary erasure channel. A specific focus is on three unique degree distributions, which are utilized in an irregular LDPC construct. The theoretical maximum final error probability of these constructions is determined using the density evolution method, and this understanding is demonstrated through a practical decoding process involving an LDPC ensemble with an increasingly large size. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of an excess degree on performance, and the trade-offs involved in designing LDPC degree distributions. Ultimately, our findings indicate that certain degree distributions with an excess degree can surpass the optimal performance of a binary repetition code, specifically in scenarios where the erasure probability is low. Additionally, we examine the density evolution process at different stages of decoding, and the resulting outcomes may be applicable to other types of irregular degree distributions. Overall, our research provides a foundation for exploring other degree-related LDPC ensembles and their potential superior performance in noise-prone channels. Finally, we investigate the practical application of these codes through an experiment involving an LDPC decoder implemented using a Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA). The results of this experiment, along with those obtained from simulation trials, are presented and compared, and the accompanying discussion highlights the benefits of using actual hardware demonstrations. Our findings indicate that if the randomization is only partially effective, a variety of attacks can be launched, including the angular multiplexing attack, which could compromise approximately 50% of the system's security. By applying graph theory to point cloud structures, we can perform operations on them that are both efficient and organized. However, certain elevations, such as those produced by Laplacian smoothing, can be problematic because they lack a key property - they are not unique. This issue arises because a given point cloud can be made up of multiple point sets that all produce the same smoothed form. To address this problem, we have developed a new technique called graph-theoretic unique smoothing, which finds a specific previous point cloud that, when smoothed, matches the smoothed form of the current point cloud. By utilizing this unique property, our method can accurately transfer the smooth features from one point cloud to another, even if they are not identical. This allows us to perform a new type of transformation, where the source point cloud and the target point cloud are defined by their smoothed forms, and this transformation is both stable and efficient. Our technique also enables us to interpret optimization problems as simple point cloud transformations. This discovery has significant implications because it shows that any problem that can be defined using graph-theoretic unique smoothing can be solved using a single smooth surface. This insight is particularly useful for solving certain classification problems, such as those involving semantic part segmentation, by transforming them into simpler form and, therefore, making them more easily solvable. This approach has been successfully applied to a dataset of human bodies and has shown great promise in our experiments. This technique also opens up the possibility of combining smooth surfaces in order to capture more complex forms and features, and this is an area that we believe warrants further exploration and research. Existing approaches, although achieving high accuracy in evaluation tasks, often rely on high-complexity representations that hinder interpretability and may incorporate sensitive personal data. Current Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) primarily focus on generating single high-quality images or continuous sequences like paragraphs. However, these models often fail to capture the intricate structure of documents that contain opposing views, such as news articles with opposing op-eds. To address this limitation, we introduce SparseGAN, a novel document GAN that incorporates an innovative sparse attention mechanism within the generator. This approach allows for the creation of document datasets containing view switches by leveraging a prototype-based discriminator. We evaluate SparseGAN through a dataset created from Wikipedia articles, and our results indicate its superiority over conventional GANs. Furthermore, we explore the semantic coherence of samples produced by SparseGAN and find them to be remarkably coherent. Additionally, we examine the sparsity of our model's attention weights and discover they facilitate easier adversarial training. We make our code and dataset publicly available to facilitate future research. Interestingly, we observe that the challenging nature of SparseGAN's training regime leads to a robust model that generalizes well. We also find that the time spent on easy positive samples during training is inversely correlated with the model's performance. To mitigate this challenge, we propose a range of improvements that result in substantial improvements over the baseline. On the other hand, the simplicity of our proposed approach is an advantage as it allows us to achieve state-of-the-art performance on a text classification task without the risk of performance degradation. Overall, our results indicate that SparseGAN yields highly coherent samples with a view structure that matches the training data. We also explore the possibility of applying this model to datasets containing multiple views and find it can produce documents with opposing views similar in nature to those in the training data. The idea of interstellar panspermia, suggesting microorganisms could survive travel between stars, has significant implications for the origins of life on Earth and potential contamination risks for future Mars missions.  To better understand this concept's validity, we need to examine three key factors: the durability of life outside a host planet, the presence of life-bearing planets capable of launching microorganisms into space, and the ability of these extracellular microorganisms to survive the journey to another star.  While the first factor is the subject of ongoing astrobiological research, the second factor is tied to the discovery of life on other planets, a topic for future study.  It is the third factor, involving the transmission of microorganisms through interstellar space, that is the focus of our analysis.  To assess this factor's viability, we consider several scenarios, including the effects of nearby supernovae on planetary systems, fast-moving molecular jets, and the harsh conditions of red dwarf star environments.  Using established metrics for radiation tolerance and genetic mutation rates, we evaluate the chances of microorganisms surviving the journey to Earth from nearby stars.  Our analysis reveals that the viability of interstellar panspermia depends on a variety of factors, including the characteristics of the delivery planet, the characteristics of the star to which microorganisms are transmitted, and the duration of their journey.  While our investigation found that the delivery of microorganisms to Earth from nearby stars is unlikely, there are some exceptions, such as the possibility of transferring microorganisms to Earth from the planet Gliese 121G b and the possibility of transferring microorganisms from Earth to the planet K2-18 c. Ultimately, investigating interstellar panspermia is essential to fully comprehend the risks and benefits associated with the transmission of life between stars. The integration of computer science and topology through topological data analysis has yielded substantial insights into understanding complex structures and shapes in various datasets. By combining computer science and algebraic geometry, we can unlock the geometric underpinnings of computational processes. In this work, we establish a geometric framework for computing answers to queries in relational databases by interpreting computation as an interpolation problem on a constructible set. This framework provides a common basis for understanding both the algorithmic and geometric aspects of computation. Furthermore, it enables the application of techniques from algebraic geometry and geometry to evaluate the computational effects of operations on data and to determine the points corresponding to computable quantities, such as the maximum or minimum of a function. This research is a follow-up to our prior work establishing the computational properties of queries computed using DPLL solvers, and it expands the scope of inquiry to include relational algebra, database queries, and solvers for nonlinear equations and constraints, such as Gröbner bases and CSP solvers. In particular, we show that the computation of answers to queries involves the construction of a fiber constructible set, and we analyze the impacts of algebraic operations on constructible sets, yielding new perspectives on the computation of points, the determination of computability, and the assessment of the complexity of queries. These insights are demonstrated through our examination of basic database queries, such as self-joins and transitive closures, and they provide a foundation for exploring the computational effects of operations on data and the development of query optimization techniques based on algebraic geometry. Additionally, we introduce an open-source Python library, called Geocomputing, that enables users to define computation graphs, identify points of interest, and determine computability by examining the topology of computation, and we apply this library to analyze several database queries and computation scenarios, such as the evaluation of expressions, the computation of fixed points, and the analysis of program dependencies and loops. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-driven generation. In this setup, hyper-prompts serve as additional input to self-attention modules, enabling them to focus on relevant input elements. By leveraging HyperNetworks to generate these hyper-prompts, we enable flexible, learned task-conditioning without fixed pre-prompts. Our proposed architecture exhibits superior performance when compared to static prompting methods and even outperforms task-specific model fine-tuning in certain cases, as evident from our results on MNLI and SNLI datasets. Furthermore, HyperPrompt demonstrates efficient hyper-prompt learning, achieving significant gains with a significantly reduced number of parameters compared to fully task-conditioned models. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt.

In simulations of complex astrophysical phenomena involving compact objects, where the gravitational field is strong, the information about the initial conditions that must be provided at the boundary between the numerical simulation and the flat spacetime is severely constrained by the Cauchy stability theorem. This limits the accuracy of the initial data solution. To circumvent this issue, the Conformal Transverse Traceless decomposition has been adapted to represent the initial perturbations as a sum of two decoupled components, one driven by the conformal piece and the other by the transverse traceless piece. While the conformal piece can cause instabilities, the transverse traceless decomposition remains stable and can be controlled, making it an ideal tool for addressing the constraints imposed by the Cauchy stability theorem. This technique can be employed to develop new methods for generating a wide range of perturbations in numerical relativity simulations, and its potential applications are discussed in the context of simulating quasioptical oscillations in neutron star mergers. The technique is also shown to be compatible with the Advanced Numerical Relativity Simulations (ANARES), and simulations are performed to evaluate its effectiveness. The results demonstrate the utility of this technique in extending the scope of numerical relativity simulations beyond the limitations imposed by the Cauchy stability theorem. The code and simulations detailed in this study have been made publicly available on the ANARES website. The novel technique presented here is a viable alternative to the Black Hole Simulation Code, and the new simulations presented here are a valuable addition to the ANARES dataset. The new simulations correspond to the black hole-neutron star merger scenario described in [1], with the exception of the neutron star mass, which is set at 1.4 solar masses. The parameters for this scenario are consistent with those reported in [2] and [3]. The results of the simulations are comparable to those obtained with the standard numerical relativity method but with fewer constraints on the initial data. The technique allows for the generation of more flexible initial data, which includes a wider range of perturbations, as demonstrated in the case of the neutron star merger simulation presented here. The use of this technique makes it possible to generate simulations with a wider range of perturbations, which is essential for accurately modeling the behavior of complex astrophysical phenomena involving compact objects. Recently, pre-trained models have dominated the field of computer vision, and knowledge distillation has become a popular technique to leverage these models by other teachers. Most current multi-teacher knowledge distillation methods can be formulated as an iterative process of average-based logits aggregation, which is mathematically equivalent to a second-order iteration under the assumption of independent and identically distributed data. However, this approach overlooks the differences in data distributions among batches, resulting in inefficient iteration. To address this limitation, we introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Aggregation (PILE) as a new, flexible framework for multi-teacher knowledge distillation. PILE treats each batch as an independent unit and uses a pairwise comparison method to combine the predictions from different teachers. We further develop an iterative strategy to optimize the loss function under the assumption of independent and identically distributed data. The proposed PILE achieves superior performance compared to the baseline methods across four benchmark datasets, and the code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/PILE. This paper addresses a type of global hindrance problem, where the primary obstacle is a solution to a specific second-order differential equation. The underlying differential equation must satisfy specific exponential and sub-quadratic growth conditions. Our main objective is to demonstrate that any solution to this global hindrance problem, given certain initial conditions within a specific range, is ultimately characterized by a uniform constant over the entire domain of definition. This constant determines the precise structure of solutions to the underlying differential equation. In turn, it plays a crucial role in establishing the uniformity outcomes of solutions to the global hindrance problem. Our main achievement is to establish that solutions to the underlying differential equation with certain exponential and sub-quadratic growth conditions can exhibit a variety of different outcomes, including both uniqueness and non-uniqueness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these outcomes are mutually exclusive, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for solutions to the underlying differential equation. On the other hand, our results imply that the outcome of solutions to a significant class of parabolic and elliptic hindrance problems can be either unique or non-unique. Additionally, we explore the concept of a solution set for solutions to the underlying differential equation, which can be either discrete or dense. Lastly, we discuss the applicability of our results to Volterra type equations and certain integro-differential equations. Our main technique involves the use of modern measure-theoretic tools, including the application of the Guo-Krasnosel'skii fixed point theorem. Our paper provides a clear and concise overview of the underlying measure-theoretic conditions required for solutions to the underlying differential equation to satisfy the specified outcome. Our main result can be viewed as an extension of a previous theorem provided by Liang and Yang in their paper on the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a specific type of Volterra equation. Our results also provide a clear and concise answer to an open question posed by Liang and Yang in their paper. This approach involves two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian, whose gradual transformation from driver to problem form allows researchers to find the target ground state. Our study reveals that quantum annealing's success depends on the Hamiltonians' interconversion paths, which must avoid sharp turns to prevent the loss of quantum coherence. We demonstrate that even minor non-stoquastic conversions can severely impede quantum annealing's efficacy, causing coherence loss and misleading the success indicator. However, we also find that environmental decoherence can sometimes serve as a disentanglement indicator, enabling the identification of suitable annealing schedules that produce target states with high fidelity. The proposed techniques offer insights into designing and executing efficient quantum annealing, overcoming the challenges posed by complex conversion paths. Furthermore, we observe that certain multi-step conversions, although causing significant coherence loss at each step, can still yield high-fidelity target states with proper delay times, serving as a basis for improving efficient quantum annealing in complex graphs. This essay explores the life and contributions of Pieter Johannes van Rhijn, a distinguished Dutch astronomer, and his role in furthering Adriaan van Maanen's and Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn's astronomical endeavors. Born in 1881, van Rhijn demonstrated exceptional aptitude in mathematics and astronomy, which led him to become associated with Kapteyn's Astronomical Laboratory. There, he became integral to the GNAB (General Nebular Abundance of Bytes) project, which aimed to determine the composition of typical star systems. After serving as director of the laboratory from 1921 to 1945, van Rhijn made notable contributions to the planning of the Second Cape Astrographic Survey and the selection of areas for the Kapteyn Project. His work laid the groundwork for subsequent investigations into the movement of the sun and the local stellar neighborhood. As the size of neural networks grows, so does the computational requirement for training them. To overcome this limitation, a popular solution involves splitting the neural network across multiple GPUs within a distributed computing system, enabling parallel processing. However, this approach presents a significant hurdle in achieving effective learning rates across the network's interconnected layers. To address this challenge, we developed a proprietary algorithm, dubbed Regional Dropout, which is unique to model-parallel learning settings. By distinctively applying dropout techniques to specific regional layers, we found that Regional Dropout substantially boosts the number of successful region combinations, from which we derive a measure of diversity. This diversity, in turn, serves as a robust indicator for optimal learning rates, adaptive regularization, and even ensembles of models. Notably, our method exhibits exceptional performance when compared to standard dropout techniques, particularly on convolutional neural networks. To facilitate seamless learning with model-parallel techniques, we also established a training program for experienced deep learning practitioners, which covers the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of Regional Dropout. This training program's effectiveness is demonstrated through a comprehensive evaluation, comprising an extensive distributed dataset, which showcases the significant improvements achieved with Regional Dropout. Furthermore, our findings highlight the immense potential for further exploration in model-parallel learning, and we openly share the models and data collected during this study. With the growing prevalence of big neural networks, our work paves the way for the development of more complex neural networks, capable of achieving even higher performance levels. In line with the deep learning community's collaborative spirit, we openly share our training program, which we believe will contribute to the advancement of model-parallel learning. This training program's success serves as an inspiration for future challenges, and we hope it will motivate others to participate in similar initiatives. As the field of deep learning continues to evolve, we anticipate the development of more innovative techniques, and we are confident that our work will endure as a landmark achievement in the history of model-parallel learning. We showcase a record of 8 decibel in resolving power when measuring a unknown single-unit phase shift, exceeding the performance of our classical counterparts. Furthermore, we highlight the potential of this architecture to tackle complex measurement challenges, such as identifying an unknown relative phase between two distinct pairs of entangled fields. Our system maintains its quantum advantage even when complex transformations are applied to the light fields, as demonstrated through measurements of phase shifts in separate locations within the resonators and upon different reflection rounds. These findings confirm the dual-cavity setup's capability to tackle intricate, spatially dispersed problems, unlocking its vast potential for solving complex dynamical problems in interconnected networks of light fields. Our research also paves the way for addressing dynamical problems in complex circuits, such as the measurement of an unknown rotation period in a light interacting with a multi-level atom in a high-Q resonator.

Effective negation understanding is crucial for comprehensive language grasping, yet the majority of existing reading comprehension datasets either gloss over or inadequately address the complex nature of negation.
To address this shortfall, we have developed CONDAQA, a comprehensive English dataset designed to evaluate the ability of models to reason about negation in a sentence-by-sentence context.
CONDAQA comprises 20,000 question-answer pairs drawn from diverse sources, including academic texts and fiction, carefully crafted to demand a thorough understanding of negation in each sentence for a correct answer.
The dataset is meticulously designed with four categories of negation cues, including explicit words, implied negation, scope, and negated conditions, covering a wide range of negation types.
Our evaluation results indicate a significant negation understanding performance gap between human and current state-of-the-art models, with CONDAQA offering valuable insights and a substantial challenge for the community to develop more effective negation understanding methods. However, these techniques require precise control of layer separation, which is challenging for cuprate superconductors with charge density waves. Here, we propose a mathematical framework and a numerical method to extract useful information from interlayer conduction measurements, even in the presence of charge density oscillations. By applying our approach to existing layer-by-layer measurement data of Tl-2201, a cuprate superconductor, we uncover evidence of enhanced conduction at particular layer separations, and identify an interlayer conduction tunneling barrier with a height of approximately 0.25 eV. Our model also considers the impact of charge density oscillations on conduction and suggests that superconducting correlations extend beyond nearest-neighbor layers. These findings provide a foundation for reinterpreting existing layer-by-layer measurement data and will facilitate future investigation of interlayer conduction in cuprate superconductors. Furthermore, our model is versatile and can be adapted to analyze conduction in other materials with layered structures. The code utilized in this research is available upon request. Phylogenetic reconstruction from genetic data is a well-established practice, 
and various methods can generate tree estimates along with confidence measures 
such as posterior probabilities or bootstrap support values, labeling the edges 
with this information. However, interpreting these results is complicated by 
the absence of a clear theoretical understanding of edge labels under different 
retreeability models. In this work, we introduce a general framework for 
defining tai-maps, which are mappings that assign labels to ordered subtrees of a 
phylogeny, building on the concept of admissible tai-maps introduced by Amenta 
and Stolfi. We demonstrate that almost all finite phylogenies have the property 
that any admissible tai-map for which the label on the root edge is zero can be 
transformed into a corresponding tai-map under a specific permutation, which 
we refer to as the adverse tai mapping. This theorem is applicable to edge 
labeling schemes, including maximum likelihood estimates and Bayesian posterior 
probabilities. As a result, our theory provides a way to analyze the behavior of 
these labeling schemes under retreeability. In addition, our framework enables 
us to explore other labeling schemes, such as Bayesian posterior probabilities 
under a constant tree length model. This research is an extension of our prior 
work presented at ALENEX 2022.

Multi-encoder models that incorporate a grid of entrances allow a model to focus on specific local details within an input, however they pose a challenge because they are inherently unselective. This unselectivity leads to difficulties such as overfitting, needing multiple entrances, and a significant increase in model size. Our proposed module, a dynamic entrance layer, overcomes these challenges by selectively leveraging certain input elements. We implemented this layer within a grid-based encoder setup, known as the dynamic entrance grid (DIG), which achieved exceptional results in multiple experiments involving text-based classification tasks, significantly outperforming both standard transformers and the existing attention-based grid encoder models that promote selection. The DIG model also exhibits a notable advantage of having a significantly smaller model size compared to its grid encoder counterparts. The code for the proposed model has been made publicly available on GitHub at the time of submission. 

In more detail, our proposed module builds upon the global mean pooling layer by incorporating an affine transformation to refine the model's selection. We experiment with two variants of this layer: a soft variant with a small additional parameter count and a hard variant with no additional parameters, which allows the model to focus on the most representative elements of the input. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This model assesses hypothetical deviations from general relativity's predictions, specifically examining how variations in the PPN gamma parameter affect measurements of stellar parallaxes, obtained from missions similar to Gaia, assuming a certain level of error. Computational simulations investigate how a range of possible values for gamma, combined with other measurement uncertainties, influence the estimation of parallax. The study finds that even in ideal experimental conditions, a significant dispersion in estimated parallax results from the varying gamma value. Consequently, the study suggests controlling for the effect of gamma on parallax estimation by utilizing intermediate-mass stars with well-determined properties, as their light curves can be modeled based on post-Newtonian theory, while also being susceptible to variations in gamma. The resulting correction for gamma then facilitates more accurate estimation of parallax for other stars. The study presents empirical data on how this correction affects the estimation of other astronomical constants, including the mass of the sun, the density of baryons, and the cosmological constant. The findings indicate a need for incorporating post-Newtonian physics into the analysis of high-accuracy astronomical data, as well as the interpretation of mission results from Gaia and similar missions. The study also offers new Gaia science goals related to the PPN gamma parameter. The PPN gamma value previously determined from astronomical data has been confirmed by highly accurate tests of general relativity in systems of compact stars and black holes. The current study sets a new, more stringent requirement for validating the value of gamma, as well as all post-Newtonian parameters, by demonstrating the necessity of validating them against multiple parallaxes obtained from missions like Gaia, as well as from other experiments, such as Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based observations of standard candles and cepheids, using Gaia-like astrometry. The study also highlights the importance of investigating post-Newtonian physics with all available and forthcoming high-accuracy astronomical data, as well as the unique capability of missions like Gaia to validate general relativity in its entirety. The research provides a new framework for investigating post-Newtonian physics using a multi-messenger approach, as well as new opportunities for cross-checking and validating fundamental post-Newtonian parameters against different observational evidence. The study also sets a new benchmark for the precision of validating the PPN gamma parameter, as well as all post-Newtonian parameters, as well as new requirements and challenges for the interpretation of general relativity

In one-dimensional discrete quantum systems with short-range interactions, a new class of self-sustaining waves called self-boosted solitons exists. These waves maintain their form without external influences by receiving a continuous, low-intensity "boost" from nearby sites. This phenomenon occurs naturally at any speed within a system's overall bandwidth and can be understood through a representation that transforms the discrete system into a equivalent continuous one. This representation reveals the requirements necessary for a self-boosted soliton to exist and it shows that these solutions are topologically protected, meaning they are resistant to changes in system parameters. Self-boosted solitons can also be created and destroyed at specific locations within a system, providing a new mechanism for energy transfer over long distances. These waves have implications for the understanding of non-equilibrium systems and may provide a new way to manufacture and control discrete solitons.

This research addresses the challenge of ensuring the security of machine learning (ML) models when they are trained with data from untrusted users. Our solution, a new framework called SIMC 2.0, enables an ML model to be trained while protecting itself from malicious clients that may manipulate input data. We demonstrate SIMC 2.0's effectiveness by applying it to a popular ML model, but also identify its limitations. Additionally, we explore ways to enhance training efficiency and create a new, open-source training framework called R2D2, which combines the benefits of both secure and efficient training. R2D2's performance is comparable to that of an optimized, unsecured model, while providing full protection against malicious clients. We believe R2D2 may serve as a reference design for the development of future secure ML models. Our research and analysis are supported by thorough security and performance analyses, along with new security proofs and empirical evaluations. Furthermore, we introduce a new attack technique called the "low-high injection attack" and validate the efficiency of R2D2 through practical experiments. On the other hand, we discover that SIMC 2.0 may fail to protect against highly sophisticated malicious clients and identify key limitations in current cryptographic techniques that could further enhance the security of ML models. Our research also raises new challenges for the development of secure ML models and could potentially inspire the creation of new, more secure models. Our solution could potentially be applied to other complex computational tasks in addition to ML computations and our research could potentially be applied to a wide range of ML models, including those that are widely used in various applications. Our experience with designing secure ML models has taught us the importance of closely collaborating with experts in the field and our solution could potentially benefit from the exploration of alternative design options that could further enhance its performance. Our research and analysis have provided valuable insights that could be applied to the development of other complex computational systems and our results have shown that secure ML models can be highly efficient and provide significant security benefits. Our solution has demonstrated its effectiveness in real-world applications and our research has addressed several open challenges that could further advance the development of secure ML models. Our experience with hosting competitions on secure ML model training has shown that it is a valuable area of research and our results have proven the feasibility of secure ML model training in real-world scenarios. The spiral galaxy M101, located approximately 20 million light-years from Earth, has been extensively studied with radio telescopes. A recent 319 MHz bandwidth observation of M101 with the FAST radio telescope revealed the detection of multiple high-velocity HI clouds beyond the galaxy's outer limits, as well as a newly discovered HI tail on M101's side opposite to the direction of the galaxy Abell 2415. The abundance of extragalactic HI clouds in this observation poses a low detection rate, around 10%, which is consistent with predictions from the VIRGO-Hi gas field simulations. The mass of the M101 galaxy group is estimated to be approximately 2.1 x 10^11 solar masses, and the group's gas fraction is found to be 0.04, which is a fractionally low value compared to other galaxy groups of similar mass. The detection of the HI tail in M101 suggests a past galaxy merger, which may have contributed to the formation of the massive stellar ring observed around M101. The ring's age is estimated to be around 1.2 billion years, which is significantly younger than the galaxy's other features. The ring's age determines its break-up time, which is now in the past, and as a result, the ring is no longer visible in optical light due to being dissipated by M101's gravitational field. The interaction between M101 and Abell 2415 is occurring at a highly oblique angle, which may contribute to the detection of the HI tail and surrounding clouds. The group's major axis is structured by M101's central spiral arms and a newly discovered small spiral galaxy, NGC 4605D. The detection of the HI tail and surrounding clouds in M101 adds it to the exclusive list of galaxies that have experienced tidal interactions and breaks, along with IC 1101, IC 1755, and NGC 4507. The unique features of the M101 galaxy group make it an ideal subject for further radio telescope observations. The large beam size of the FAST radio telescope allows it to make such detections possible, and the uniqueness of its observations opens up the possibility of making similar discoveries with other radio telescopes. The possible presence of HI clouds and a tail in the M101 galaxy group were first revealed by recent radio telescope observations, and further research is needed to better understand the true extent and characteristics of these features, as well as the history and dynamics of the M101 galaxy group. To effectively handle questions without context, a significant issue in current approaches is their overreliance on surface-level information, which is addressed through the proposal of a novel semantic-related insight framework. This proposed framework divides the question-answering process into two stages: a coarse stage and a precise stage. In the coarse stage, a strategy is suggested to narrow down the answer choices to a limited set based on general, high-level information. For the precise stage, a new approach is proposed to further refine the choices by considering more specific, semantically-related aspects. This two-stage approach is tested on the Open-QA dataset, and the results show improved performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the proposed framework is found to be flexible and adaptable to other question-answering tasks. Additionally, the paper introduces the Open-QA Relational dataset, which introduces explicit relational information between answers on the original dataset, and uses this dataset to evaluate the proposed framework. The results from different subtasks demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in addressing the semantic-related issue in open-domain question answering. The paper is also unique in its use of a new evaluation metric called the relative absolute error, which measures the performance of the proposed framework in selecting the correct answer from a set of options. A comprehensive analysis of cometary atmospheres relies heavily on accurate and complete spectra of essential molecular ions. A critical category includes oxygen-containing species such as aldehydes, ketones, and organic acids, which are crucial components of cometary gas-phase chemistry despite existing spectrum gaps in this field. A potentially explanatory factor for these gaps is identified by examining previously studied ion spectra under simulated cometary conditions and focusing on those containing oxygen, where notable gaps are found among aldehydes, ketones, and organic acids with lower molecular weights. These deficiencies could limit interpretation of cometary spectra and subsequent kinetic modeling of cometary atmospheres; as an example, existing models of C2H4O and C2H6O interpretations are assessed for such gaps, revealing potential for underestimation of reactant concentrations due to model limitations. As such, a call is made for spectral studies or theoretical calculations of these deficient species to enhance our understanding of cometary chemistry. Furthermore, it is proposed that in the absence of such data, existing models could be refined to account for potential biases and overestimation of product concentrations when comparing them to observations from astrophysical environments. This call for action is particularly relevant in light of upcoming space missions that will significantly improve the analysis of cometary spectra and corresponding kinetic modeling. As such, a framework for model improvements is provided, emphasizing the importance of accuracy in spectral databases and the value of open communication and data sharing among researchers in this field. This study explores the concept of square sums in global fields, specifically focusing on expressions of the form $\sum_{a \in \mathcal{O}_K} a^2$ for fields of degree $1$ and $2$. We are able to show that this sum can be expressed as a norm-based expression, and through this, we establish links to earlier research. Additionally, this study provides calculations for square sums in quadratic fields with an appropriate ideal in the ring of integers, expanding on earlier results in this area. Furthermore, we establish connections between square sums and the trace function, and through this, we derive formulas for square sums in quadratic fields without an appropriate ideal in the ring of integers. These connections also enable us to pose questions and hypotheses regarding the behavior of square sums in higher-degree extensions. Finally, we establish and prove a conjecture regarding square sums in cubic fields with an appropriate ideal in the ring of integers. This conjecture links the square sum to the trace function and provides calculations for square sums in cubic fields without an appropriate ideal in the ring of integers. High-dimensional spectral data from photonic sources and astronomical observations are often cross-referenced with catalog entries for various applications including photonic lensing, star identification, and active galaxy research. The traditional approach uses standard techniques such as nearest neighbors, discriminant analysis, and tree division but can be limiting due to their rigid nature, requiring significant scaling for each new problem. This occurs in part because these methods are inherently inconsistent with the continuous, linear nature of spectral data. We introduce two innovative methods, based on photonics-specific features, addressing these limitations. Our first method, SpectrumEmbedding, uses a data-driven approach to capture the unique patterns in spectral data and overcomes the inconsistencies mentioned above. Our second method, SpectrumTree, combines elements of decision trees and spectral embedding to create a more efficient and scalable algorithm for cross-referencing. We showcase the effectiveness of these methods by applying them to the CHASMs dataset containing active galaxy spectra. Our results indicate that SpectrumEmbedding and SpectrumTree achieve superior performance compared to traditional techniques and even outperform methods developed specifically for scalable embedding on this particular dataset. Furthermore, we highlight the versatility of these methods by employing them to identify new features in the CHASMs dataset. Our work demonstrates the potential for photonic-based methods to enhance cross-referencing techniques, making it an exciting area for further exploration and research in both astrophysics and machine learning. The precise interaction of medications affects how they interact, meaning that certain combinations may have adverse effects or be ineffectual. Deep learning's ability to examine complex relationships is appealing for studying these interactions. Nonetheless, medications are often represented as sequential one-dimensional entities with limited inherent semantic meaning. This lack of semantic foundation poses difficulties for traditional relational deep learning methods when applying them to medication pair scoring tasks. Our research provides a semantic-based cohesive framework that can effectively capture the intricate relationships between medications when combined. This combined representation maintains a balance between semantic and relational information, using a range-based scoring function that considers both elements. Our model's ability to accurately predict the precision of medication combinations has been demonstrated, with results showing a 6.57% improvement in overall accuracy when tested against a leading benchmark dataset. This proposed model offers a versatile, semantic-based approach that can be adapted for use in various medication combination prediction tasks. This paper introduces a novel approach, Federated Learning from Diversified Walks (FLDW), which leverages random strolls of students to enhance teacher learning on a diverse dataset. FLDW addresses several challenges faced by existing federated learning frameworks, including the limited quality of student updates, the high communication cost, and the risk of data leakage. By incorporating random strolls, FLDW procures a affordable and high-quality training experience for students, enabling them to engage in frequent updates with the teacher. We evaluate FLDW through FLDW Walks and a modified Split-Batch strategy, both of which demonstrate its effectiveness and efficiency in training models from datasets with diverse samples. Our experiments showcase the versatility of FLDW, applying it to the training of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for both image and text classification tasks. The criminal justice system is facing a mental health crisis within its own ranks. To better comprehend the mental well-being of defendants and the effectiveness of court-ordered treatment, this paper conducts a statistical analysis of mental health diagnoses among defendants before and after trial, including both those who received court-ordered treatment and those who did not. Our findings reveal that defendants experience heightened mental health issues following their involvement in the criminal justice system, with diagnosis rates increasing by more than 15% after trial. Interestingly, we discover that the enhanced mental health issues persist for both groups, with no difference in diagnosis rates between defendants who received court-ordered treatment and those who did not, likely due to limitations in our data that preclude differentiation between types of treatment. Our research also explores various aspects of the defendant population, including different genders, age groups, and defendants charged with violent crimes, finding that the increased mental health issues persist across these subgroups as well. Our study offers a starting point for exploring the complex relationship between court-ordered treatment and the mental well-being of defendants, with implications for the design of treatment programs that can provide long-lasting mental health benefits for those involved in the criminal justice system. Our preliminary findings are based on publicly available data from federal court cases in the United States between 2009 and 2020. Our analysis highlights the difficulties associated with conducting causal research on the impact of court-ordered treatment on the mental well-being of defendants, with potential solutions discussed. Our data and code are publicly available for replication and extension by other researchers. Our study is a first step in a broader research project that aims to examine the mental health issues within the criminal justice system and the effectiveness of court-ordered treatment, with a focus on federal court cases in the United States. However, the underlying concepts and research questions are relevant to other jurisdictions and court systems, with potential applications to other countries and court systems. A widespread issue in medical image segmentation, especially under semi-supervised conditions, is the reliance on over-complicated models that are prone to consistent performance when faced with new data. This problem is addressed by presenting an uncommonly simple regularization technique for semi-supervised segmentation, characterized by minimal additional parameters. This technique utilizes a model that is trained on labeled data and an encoder that is trained on unlabelled data, with the aim of producing identical outputs for the same input images. No additional loss functions are employed, instead utilizing existing loss functions for optimization. Our proposed technique is evaluated on two publicly available datasets, with notable improvements achieved when compared to the segmentation model's baseline performance. The ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system features a fully integrated, 32-bit issue speedup circuit called the Link Module, which connects the Calorimeter Trigger Processor units. This Link Module circuit is built using the Ultrascale+ FPGA and operates at a velocity of nearly 1 Gbps per bit, setting a industry record for 32-bit data transfer. This high transfer rate is achieved with a novel data encoding method called the "alternating bi-directional" encoding, also enabling reduced electrical interference and data errors. Furthermore, the circuit has been designed with low dependency on clock distribution methods, ensuring its robustness and adaptability for use in complex, large-scale systems like the ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system. This project's innovative approach to high-speed data transfer may be adapted for other applications requiring fast data transfer, such as the CMS Phase-1 muon trigger system and the future HEP systems with end-to-end data transfer. This work is being presented at the 2019 IEEE Symposium on Field-Programmable Custom Computing Machines. Recent advances in exact quantum state simulation via quantum neutral network models have created opportunities for fundamental science breakthroughs. Our research proposes a novel application of these models, using an interpretable graph neural network for quantum dynamics simulation. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness in identifying and quantifying complex phenomena, such as mixing and order, in one-dimensional hydrogen atom time-series data. This approach leverages a fixed graph structure that reflects the spatial relationships defined by the underlying Hamiltonian, allowing for the extraction of temporally localized and interpretable signatures of quantum dynamics. Our framework is tested against a realistic scenario involving the simulation of one-dimensional hydrogen atom time-series data, and it shows that it can accurately capture both local and global properties of the system's evolution. Furthermore, we investigate the semantic similarity between the learned representations and their connection to the underlying physical principles, using both quantitative and qualitative analysis. Our results indicate that the learned representations not only capture the spatial symmetry of the system's behavior but also the temporal symmetry, and we observe a semantic similarity between the learned tokens that corresponds to the system's conserved quantities. Our research also highlights potential challenges and opportunities for further exploration, and it paves the way for the development of more sophisticated neural network models that can provide a deeper understanding of the intricate relationships between quantum dynamics, geometry, and symmetry. In cases where data falls into multiple categories or is derived from several separate groups, determining the maximum likelihood estimate of the average of the respective parameters becomes a complex task. A notable challenge arises when these individual groups are not fully observed, as only partial information about them is available through a mixture distribution. The problem is particularly prevalent in statistics when collecting samples from a population that has undergone a transformation, as it then consists of gathering data from multiple mixtures. The Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimate of a mixture parameter, developed in this paper, provides an innovative solution for assessing the average of parameters in such scenarios. Through simulation, we demonstrate the efficacy of this new estimator, GMLAE, in comparing its performance to existing competitors. The estimated methods are also tested on real-world data sets to illustrate their applicability. This research is particularly useful for its broad applications, including but not limited to, the evaluation of population parameters in statistics, the assessment of radiation levels in environmental samples, and the determination of proportions in clinical trials. These verification tasks often generate proof files containing the sequence of steps used to demonstrate program correctness, which can be used to derive the underlying model or proof of correctness. However, current SMT proofs and model representations have limitations, including a lack of expressiveness and readability, which hinders their effectiveness in the verification process. This issue is further exacerbated by the limited support for quantifier reasoning and proof flattening in SMT solvers, which leaves gaps in the proof structure, making it difficult to establish the desired properties of a program or function. Recently, massive datasets have facilitated self-supervised pre-training for end-to-end ASR models, significantly improving performance. Nonetheless, such benefits are largely confined to similar languages and fine-tuning tasks. To bridge gaps between languages and task levels, we propose two main strategies: a) using a coarse model that can handle a broad range of languages with minimal adaptation, and b) leveraging cross-lingual transfer learning. By combining these approaches, we've achieved notable advancements in ASR accuracy for both low-resampling rates and languages other than English, with the former improving by ~11% absolute relative improvement and the latter by ~5% ARI. On the latter front, our results show that a fine English model outperforms all other baselines by ~5% ARI on the TIMIT dataset. Moreover, our method has yielded a mean ARI of ~5% on the 100-Linguos dataset and a mean absolute improvement of ~2% on resampling rates of 8 kHz. Furthermore, our method has proven that a pre-trained model with 1 billion parameters can achieve ~5% ARI better than a 50-million parameter model on the 100-Linguos dataset. Evaluating graph neural network node representations in social networks is a challenging task due to the absence of ground truth data. Our research presents TwitchPlayers, a diverse and publicly available dataset featuring 2D embeddings of 368 Opencorporates.org's legal person entities, derived from their Wikipedia pages. These entities, constituting approximately 7% of all Canadian corporations, are represented in a social network with 12,375 nodes and a clear hierarchical structure. Our findings highlight the limitations of current evaluation methods and highlight the utility of TwitchPlayers for assessing the structural and topological preservation capabilities of node representations learned through graph neural networks. This dataset enables the rigorous examination of a network's internal structure and its external projections, providing insight into the effectiveness of graph neural networks at capturing a social network's underlying characteristics. Our research is an essential step in the development of more robust evaluation metrics for node representations in social networks. Our work with this dataset highlights the limitations of current evaluation methods and the benefits of a more holistic approach, and our code and dataset are available for further exploration and advancement. Our research with TwitchPlayers includes an analysis of the qualitative and quantitative aspects of this dataset, as well as the application of this dataset to the development of a new evaluation metric. This study is an important contribution to the field of graph neural networks and social network analysis, and our results with TwitchPlayers are a key achievement in the evaluation of node representations learned through graph neural networks. Our study proposes that the $1.5$ GeV spin-triplet state commonly referred to as $f_J(1500)$ in various hadronic decays, specifically in $B\to \pi(K)KK$ decays, actually makes up a rice paddy-like structure and could be a component state of $\rho^0(1450)$. To verify this hypothesis, a comprehensive mathematical framework is developed to interpret the observed decay patterns from an analytical perspective. Our calculations reveal that if $\rho^0(1450)$ exists with the desired mass and other characteristics, its contribution could account for around $80\%$ of the total decay rate of $f_J(1500)$ in $B\to K\bar{K}$ decays. Furthermore, our study identifies two possible explanations for the differing rates of decay into $\rho^0$ and $\omega$, and it demonstrates that the observed decay patterns can be accounted for by considering decay processes at the level of quark composition, rather than relying on meson factorization. As a result, our study supports the notion that $\rho^0(1450)$ is, in fact, the underlying state that gives rise to the characteristics of $f_J(1500)$. Additionally, our research provides new production and decay channel predictions for $\rho^0(1450)$ in both $B$ and $C$ decays. If confirmed experimentally, this study will lead to a reevaluation of existing experimental analyses of $B$ and $C$ decays at energies around $1.5$ GeV. Moreover, our study demonstrates that $\rho^0(1450)$ can be searched for in a dedicated experiment involving $B$ and $C$ decays at heavy-flavor factories such as Belle-II, BEPCII, and LHCb, where potential experimental evidence could be found in as little as $5$ to $10$ fb$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity. This paper presents a novel approach to achieving accurate force control in series elastic actuators (SEAs) through a transmission force observer (TFO) using a strong form. The limitations of SEA feedback systems are examined, and the concept of the TFO is introduced as a means to accurately estimate the actuator's force output. A theoretical framework for the TFO is developed and its performance evaluated in comparison to alternative methods. A practical implementation of the TFO is demonstrated in a practical SEA setup, and its effectiveness validated through experimental results. The benefits of the proposed method are highlighted through closed-loop stability analysis and a discussion on the relevant practical considerations is included. The approach is applicable to SEA systems with rigidly connected loads and enables precise force control with a fast closed-loop system. Experimental data corresponds to the SEA setup provided in the supplementary materials. The approach is also suitable for SEA systems with stiff transmission elements and has been successfully demonstrated in collaboration with the robotics group at the University of Colorado Boulder. The associated code is available under the name sea_force_control at https://git.rg.crc.edu/robotics-lab/sea_force_control. The paper also includes an open issue regarding the sensitivity of the TFO and several possible approaches to address it. The issue can be found in section IV.A and the possible solutions in section V.A. To ensure the safety of underwater robots, predicting the movements of marine animals is crucial. Underwater robots must anticipate and adapt to the changing swimming patterns of these animals as they navigate through the water. By assuming the water remains calm and undisturbed, we can apply Gaussian Process regression to forecast the animals' position based on their past swimming patterns. However, this approach fails to account for the possibility of water turbulence affecting the animals' movement. To address this limitation, we enhance Gaussian Process regression with additional factors such as the animals' speed and orientation in the water. By modeling these factors as stationary processes that vary over time, we can combine them with the original Gaussian Process model. This integrated model allows the estimation of a covariance function for the animals' movement, taking into consideration both the effects of water turbulence and the animals' internal states. By utilizing this covariance function in Bayesian filtering, we can make more accurate predictions about the animals' movement, their swimming speed, and their orientation in the water. Our proposed method outperforms the established methods for our demonstration scenario, proving its effectiveness in forecasting the swimming patterns of marine animals. Furthermore, we demonstrate our method's applicability to the prediction of multiple animals' movements by applying it to the swimming patterns of both dolphins and sea lions. Our research demonstrates that water turbulence has a significant impact on marine animals' swimming patterns and confirms the utility of our approach in real-world scenarios. By evaluating our model's performance using both simulated and actual data, we validate its capability in predicting the swimming patterns of marine animals accurately. Our proposed method has the potential to be utilized in the monitoring of marine animals' behavior, particularly in the detection of abnormal swimming patterns, and is suitable for deployment on an underwater computer. Our research data and code are available for use and review. This paper introduces Arrangement Networks (ANets) that efficiently capture
self-similarity within data by utilizing constant-depth neural network architecture.
ANets apply pair-based processing to sequentially generate an ordering of increasing
similarity among input data points. We demonstrate how ANets can be trained in an
unsupervised and distributed manner, resulting in a robust representation that
performs exceptionally well across various benchmark tasks, even when compared to
more complex neural network models like Autoencoders and Transformers. Furthermore,
ANets excel particularly in embedding data with temporal or hierarchical relationships. 

For high-dimensional feature extraction, ANets outperform existing methods in models
like Support Vector Machines and K-Means, and even surpass non-neural network techniques
like Multidimensional Scaling. Additionally, ANets exhibit exceptional performance
in generative tasks such as sample generation and missing value imputation.

Galactic mergers are a primary driver in the development and transformation of galaxies throughout the universe, as stated by multiple cosmological simulations. This study explores how magnetic fields affect gas and stellar interactions during galaxy mergers by analyzing high-resolution, globally scalable galaxy mergers in multiple directions. Our findings show that a realistic magnetic field has little impact on the overall structure and motion of galaxy mergers, based on general features such as orbital paths, collision velocities, and the distribution of baryonic matter. However, more detailed analysis reveals some differences, including altered stellar bar formations, shifted gas distributions, and changed galaxy shapes, especially in the early stages of the merger when the galaxies are still distinct. These effects disappear as the galaxies merge further. In contrast, a significantly strong magnetic field causes magnetic flux expansion, leading to enhanced gas dissipation at orbital points and resulting in more compact, disk-shaped galaxy mergers. These results will be compared to other simulations using an ideal magnetic gas in a companion paper. Due to magnetic field strengths considered in this study still being relatively small, less than 4 uG, no evidence of electron recombination radiation or other non-thermal phenomena was found, which could further impact galaxy mergers, especially when magnetic fields are stronger. High-resolution simulations with these relatively weak magnetic fields, capable of resolving stellar bars and multi-kiloparsec gas structures, have been performed for the first time, also allowing for the emergence of magnetic field structures, such as magnetic arms, which form when galaxies merge. These newly created magnetic field structures can impact galaxy evolution, especially when magnetic fields are greater, and will be further examined in a companion paper. The legacy of this study includes the development of an ideal magnetic gas implementation for the grid-based GIZMO code and a suite of realistic galaxy merger simulations available for further research. Many languages, including Japanese, Korean, and English, suffer from written text that contains grammatical errors due to growing online content. Correcting these errors systematically is crucial, and existing research has focused on rule-based and statistical methods. Although achieved accuracy was good for specific domains, results suffered when applying the methods to new domains with little training data. This research aims to overcome this challenge by assuming a small training set is available for each new domain that needs error correction. Our approach involves using a shared model that can quickly adapt to a new domain by identifying the most effective corrections for new sentences. This led to significant improvements, and our findings show small domain-specific training is enough to reduce the number of errors by half without needing a large training set. This advantage was observed across four domains and demonstrated that our approach can correct not just grammatical errors but also style changes, and that the method is applicable to other machine learning tasks that involve few-shot learning. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghr21/meta-gerc.

Rounding is an inevitable phenomenon when reporting numbers, particularly means based on questionable data, as seen in infamous cases like the Gallup poll average of Republican voting intentions in 2000. When estimating a total using rounded values, confidence in the estimate depends on the degree of ambiguity or range represented by the reported mean. To illustrate this issue with a concrete example, consider a survey where the reported mean is 5, indicating a range of 4.5 to 5.5. If assumed to be 5 exactly, a value of  x would be acceptable, but if assumed to be 4.5 or 5.5, the acceptable value would be significantly different. To address this problem, instead of reporting a single range for a rounded mean, we propose using multiple potential estimates represented by overlapping intervals. As a proposed solution for the problem of rounded means, we develop a method for predicting voting behavior using regression models that take into account the range represented by the reported mean. Given that many real-world applications involve skewed distributions, we anticipate our method to be an effective approach for addressing the problem of rounded means. With our proposed method, we predict voting behavior using models that account for the range represented by the reported mean and compare our results to established prediction methods. Our analysis suggests that consideration of the range has a significant impact on prediction, especially in cases with skewed distributions. In conclusion, we expect our approach to be an useful solution for addressing the problem of rounded means and voting behavior prediction in general. In the context of allocating essential items to self-interested agents, where the number of items available does not exceed the number of agents, we examine two primary scenarios. Firstly, assuming a single round of simultaneous, independent action among $n$ agents, we aim to identify the pure Nash equilibria in which no agent can improve their outcome by unilaterally changing their strategy, given that the distribution mechanism is known. Secondly, with the objective of creating fair outcomes resistant to unilateral disruption, we investigate the design of mechanisms that induce equilibria in which all agents' outcomes are equal, the most basic form of fairness. Both theoretical and practical applications can benefit from an in-depth understanding of these equilibrium concepts and the development of fair, intuitive mechanisms. In the past decade, a substantial body of research has emerged on the distribution of items to self-interested agents, addressing various scenarios but distinct from the present setting in which the number of items available equals or exceeds the number of agents. The exploration of equilibrium behavior and fair mechanism design became possible only with the development of suitable new tools. The study of pure Nash equilibria and fair mechanism design was first possible only with the introduction of new graph theoretical concepts and the analysis of monotone utility functions. A fair mechanism for inducing equilibria in which all agents' outcomes are equal, as well as the characterization of pure Nash equilibria in general, result from the derivation of essential implications of the graph model and its associated utility functions. The proposed fair mechanism can be applied to any context where the distribution of items among self-interested agents is essential, and it represents one of the most basic notions of fairness, achievable with $2$ rounds of interaction between the agents and the mechanism designer. The description and analysis of our fair mechanism may also provide valuable insights on pure Nash equilibria in general settings. The term of self-publishing gives us the opportunity to share our research with the broader scientific community, and we hope this work will inspire the exploration of additional fair mechanism design problems. The design of the proposed fair mechanism has been successfully tested on real-world data, and the results it achieves are presented in the accompanying supplementary material. The data used in the study can be found in the relevant public databases. Additionally, DP-Sync fosters an innovative 'DP-bridging' concept, facilitating the integration of distinct differential privacy realizations. Two concrete implementations of DP-Sync are also explored, along with discussions on potential future developments and challenges in the field. Radio sources within globular clusters hold significant information about their members including black holes and neutron stars. However, their abundance and characteristics remain poorly understood due to limited viewing angles and cluster distances in previous observations. A new survey, the MAVERIC study, addresses these constraints by focusing on 31 radio sources within the core of the globular cluster G1 in the Andromeda galaxy using Chandra X-ray observations and cm-wave radio data from the VLA. These sources exhibit a diverse range of properties, including powerful jets from black holes with accretion, flat spectra from radio pulsars, and dim pulsars. By analyzing the spectral energy distribution of these sources with radio, X-ray, and optical data, the study distinguishes between radio pulsars, accreting black holes, and other sources. It discovers a dynamically created population of radio pulsars with characteristic ages ranging from less than one million to over 100 million years and finds that their formation efficiency from supernovae explosions is about 30%. On the other hand, it finds very few black holes with jets, much fewer than expected, and attributes this low number to the clusters' small mass rather than the cluster's rapid evolution, which would have destroyed black hole candidates. It also discovers a large die-off rate of radio pulsars with ages between one million and several billion years, likely caused by their gravitational collapse under the cluster's intense gravity rather than external factors. This understanding of radio sources in globular clusters challenges previous theories of cluster evolution and offers new insights into the history of the Andromeda galaxy. It also highlights the importance of observing radio sources in the galaxy and suggests a new approach to studying radio sources in other globular clusters in the Andromeda galaxy. The basis for building highly accurate and efficient knowledge-based systems lies in their underlying ontologies. However, creating or updating these ontologies using traditional methods is time-consuming and poses challenges for topics like COVID-19 research, which are highly dynamic. To address this issue, we employ a deep learning technique to incorporate unstructured text from online biomedical sources into existing ontologies, specifically using the BioNLP-OVA representation. Our approach, known as OntoVA, leverages BERT to classify relation mentions found in research papers and automatically add them to the ontology in the correct format. To account for entities without specified relations, OntoVA applies a relation inference strategy, leveraging both gold standard and predicted data to train and evaluate itself. The system's effectiveness was tested on the COVID-19 Ontology, resulting in the identification of over 150,000 new entities and relations within a week. Evaluation against a reference dataset showed OntoVA's high accuracy, with an F1 score of 92% for entity recognition, 83% for relation classification, and 79% for inferred relations. Quantifying uncertainty in a model's output is crucial in both human experts and machine learning models, especially when that output affects critical decisions or actions. While much research focuses on developing new uncertainty techniques, this work takes a different approach, evaluating and comparing existing methods for quantifying ambiguity in data through scientific machine intelligence, specifically mean squared error and Kullback-Leibler divergence. We examine various uncertainty quantification techniques from a mathematical perspective, discuss their application to multiple metric definitions, and provide code for their implementation in Python. Ultimately, we highlight the limitations of current measures and encourage the development of more effective techniques for assessing uncertainty in scientific machine learning. This is particularly relevant in the context of growing concerns over the reliability of AI-driven decisions, especially when those decisions are influenced by data that is uncertain or imprecise. We believe that enhancing the precision of uncertainty quantification will be essential for addressing these validity issues. In the field of scientific machine learning, models are often trained using Bayesian methods or deep neural networks that incorporate maximum likelihood estimation. The choice of uncertainty measure depends on the type of model used, with the Kullback-Leibner divergence being applicable to both. Other metrics such as the Jensen-Shannon and total variation distance are also relevant in this context. We examine the application of these methods to multiple datasets, including the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Boston housing datasets. We also explore the use of deep neural networks, incorporating the Boston housing dataset as an example. We discuss the advantages and limitations of each method, highlighting their dependence on model parameters, data characteristics, and issues with normalization. We acknowledge the guidance provided by Dr. Andrew Wilson and the support from the IBM AI Horizon CodeLab. We propose future research directions, including the development of more robust uncertainty measures that account for overfitting, the exploration of uncertainty in model selection, and the investigation of deep neural network uncertainty in the context of classification. We hope that this work will contribute to the advancement of uncertainty research in scientific machine intelligence. We have made the dataset and code available for public access through this manuscript. Further details on deep neural network uncertainty can be found in the supplementary document. We have also included the quantitative evaluation of our method in the appendix. This work has not been previously published and is not currently submitted elsewhere. This paper proposes a novel concept, a shared semantic space that is consistent across languages, and suggests a new model to achieve this concept. Our proposed model utilizes a hidden factor to represent clusters in each language, and then combines the cluster representations to create a shared semantic space. This model is mathematically sound and is trained using a hidden-factor model and a noise-contrastive estimation method. Our experiments demonstrate that this model produces a high-quality shared semantic space that is cluster-consistent, and is particularly effective in resolving the polysemy problem. Our model's performance is verified in three challenging tasks: semantic relatedness evaluation, word sense induction, and bilingual word similarity. The code for our model has been made available online. Furthermore, we introduce a rigorous evaluation metric called the cluster-consistency score to assess the consistency of a shared semantic space. This metric evaluates the degree to which the representations of the same cluster in different languages are consistent. Our model's cluster-consistency score sets a new high bar for other state-of-the-art models that are compared against it in the word similarity task. Interestingly, we observed that models with high cluster-consistency scores generally under-perform in the relatedness task. Our analysis with cluster-specific scores sheds light on the existing challenges of models that are designed to operate in a multi-lingual setting and suggests opportunities for further improvement. The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable errors in its annotated goal labels. These inaccuracies negatively impact training high-performance dialogue state tracking models. This paper undertakes a thorough examination of the sources of these label imperfections and conducts a comprehensive evaluation of the current state-of-the-art models' robustness. To build upon this, we introduce a new dataset named MultiWOZ 2.0* with corrected labels and a corresponding evaluation framework named ASSIST, which enables the assessment of models' performance in relation to label imperfections and real-world applications. Our research demonstrates the significance of developing models capable of resisting the anomalies present in poorly annotated datasets, and we share a novel architecture named MultiTask with Self-Contrast (MTSC) that achieves superior performance in dialogue state tracking tasks while being robust to label errors. This convex cone is essentially the intersection of two convex cones - the Sum of Squares (SOS) cone and the strictly positive definite (SPD) cone. Our research delves into identifying the exact boundary between the SOS cone and the new defined convex cone. On one hand, we prove that any quadratic polynomial can be expressed as a combination of a SOS polynomial and an SPD polynomial. On the other hand, we provide a general algorithm to determine whether a given cubic or higher degree polynomial can be decomposed into the combination of a SOS polynomial and an SPD polynomial. Our discussion also focuses on the computational complexity associated with this decomposition method. 

Regarding quadratic polynomials, we observe that their representation as a combination of a SOS polynomial and an SPD polynomial is always achievable. In contrast, determining whether a given quadratic polynomial can be expressed in such a manner is an NP-hard problem.
