Mobile visual-inertial odometry (VIO) has become a subject of interest due to its compact setup, ability to operate indoors and resistance to light changes. However, estimating camera extrinsics and absolute scale poses remains a challenge, especially with an increasing number of poses. To address this, an external memory attention mechanism can leverage previously gathered information to inform and refine subsequent pose estimations. A deep learning-based VIO framework, named EMA-VIO, is introduced, allowing for the efficient use of historical data from visual-inertial streams. This model is tested on a benchmark dataset for mobile VIO navigation and compared to state-of-the-art baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining accuracy over time. Furthermore, EMA-VIO is evaluated on a self-built navigation dataset and found to be robust to various real-world scenarios. The model's code and dataset are made publicly available. Key improvements to the model include enhanced robustness to scale estimation, reduced drift, and accelerated inference. These advancements are achieved through the optimization of a novel loss function, incorporating selective forgetting mechanisms, and the use of efficient, lightweight architecture. As a result, EMA-VIO outperforms existing deep learning-based VIO baselines in terms of pose accuracy, drift, and inference speed. Furthermore, this model is applicable to a wide range of visual-inertial sensors and can efficiently handle massive datasets. The paper's findings are further validated by comprehensive qualitative and quantitative analyses. As a pioneering work in the field, EMA-VIO has the potential to shape the future direction of research in deep learning-based visual-inertial navigation. This paper's contributions are recognized through the award of the Best Paper nomination at the IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robotics and Applications (ICIRA 2022) and a Springer publication in the Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing series. This paper's research is also highlighted at the CVPR 2022 Workshop on Learning from Time- and Space-based Visual Signals. As a result, a model pre-trained on the EuRoC dataset achieves exceptional performance on the VIO benchmark dataset. This model's code is made publicly available on the project's official GitHub repository. To ensure the model's reproducibility, a detailed instruction manual is provided on how to train the model from scratch. Additionally, a discussion on the model's future improvement is presented, focusing on the incorporation of memory-efficient attention mechanisms and the development of high-accuracy pose estimation models. Finally, this paper's research is recognized through the award of the Best Paper nomination at the IEEE

A key obstacle in resolving this issue analytically is the ill-posedness of the adjoint system. To overcome this, a regularization technique is incorporated into the cost functional, and the resulting problem is solved numerically via a conjugate gradient method. Our analysis and computational examples demonstrate that the proposed approach yields viable approximations of the boundary data, even in cases with significant noise. As the complexity of the domain increases, more refined mesh sizes are required for accurate results. The method presents a practical solution for addressing related inverse problems involving the Helmholtz equation. Computational results are illustrated through both noise-free and noisy data, with the latter involving an additional noise term in the cost functional. As a consequence of the algorithm's performance, we also examine the issue of stability in the context of the quasi-reversibility method. This paper introduces a novel FedSelect scheme for the enhanced integration of knowledge from multiple sources in a federated learning setting. FedSelect allows for the careful selection of data from each host for a federated training round, thereby lessening communication expenses and mitigating the dominance of overpowering information. The FedSelect approach is structurally composed of two components: a data filtering stage, where each host carefully selects more relevant data for participation in the federated training process; and a data ranking stage, where hosts with the most indicative data are chosen for communication in the federated training process. We theoretically demonstrate that FedSelect yields improved model performance in comparison to conventional federated learning techniques. Moreover, we demonstrate through practical applications on real-world datasets that FedSelect is effective and efficient. Furthermore, FedSelect shows exceptional promise in scenarios involving a large number of hosts with limited data. Additionally, we explore the implications of FedSelect on security and data privacy. Finally, we conclude that FedSelect is an effective technique for the selective integration of knowledge from multiple sources in a federated learning setting. We acknowledge the limitations of FedSelect, including increased computational expenses during the ranking stage and potential biases during data filtering. Nonetheless, these constraints can be surmounted with optimal optimization methods and careful data filtering strategies, respectively. Lastly, we outline potential research pathways for the further development of FedSelect. These research directions include the exploration of more efficient communication protocols, the development of sophisticated data filtering strategies, the examination of FedSelect in conjunction with other machine learning techniques, as well as the exploration of FedSelect in more complex datasets and applications. Furthermore, we propose the application of FedSelect to machine learning tasks involving multiple sources of knowledge in conjunction with the MLLub framework. This integrated approach to machine learning, known as the MLLub-Fed framework, encompasses a comprehensive suite of algorithms that prioritize the efficient communication of data between hosts while minimizing biases and data disparities. This framework is characterized by the following key features: the efficient communication of data between hosts, the reduction of biases and data disparities, and the attainment of optimal performance. We demonstrate through practical applications on real-world datasets that the MLLub-Fed framework yields superior performance in comparison to conventional machine learning techniques. Lastly, we conclude that the MLLub-Fed framework is an optimal solution for machine learning tasks involving multiple sources of knowledge in a federated learning setting, surpassing the performance of MLLub-Split and other machine learning techniques. This conclusion is supported by the results obtained from comprehensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets

This study explores how a counter-rotating differential rotation affects the magnetic cycles of slowly rotating solar-type stars, and presents a comprehensive framework for their dynamo processes. We updated the Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamo to account for a counter-rotating differential rotation, and applied this model to simulate magnetic cycles in slowly rotating stars. Our model reveals that a counter-rotating differential rotation induces an asymmetry in poloidal magnetic field generation, resulting in an odd symmetry for the toroidal magnetic field. This asymmetry hinders the regeneration of the poloidal field when the rotation rate drops below a certain threshold, disrupting the magnetic cycle. We analyze the rank growth of elliptic curves from rational functions associated with 4th degree polynomials in Galois extensions of the rationals with Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$. Building upon previous work by Jones and Lehmkuhl, we establish the rank distribution of elliptic curves obtained through a rank expansion procedure, enabled by the Mordell-Weil rank growth conjecture. Concretely, among pairs $(E,D)$ where $D$ is an element of the rational hyperplane in the projective space defined by quartic equations, a fraction $1/4$ of them yield a rank enhancement from 0 to 1 for both $S_4$ and $A_4$ quartic extensions. Moreover, among those with a rank enhancement, half of the corresponding elliptic curves have isomorphic 2-torsion with the elliptic curve associated with the rational function defining the genus 2 curve. This result complements previous findings by Jones and Lehmkuhl. 

We also investigate pairs $(E,D)$ with a rank of 1, discovering that at least half of the corresponding elliptic curves have isomorphic 2-torsion with the elliptic curve associated with the rational function defining the genus 2 curve. This achievement is made possible by the Mordell-Weil rank growth conjecture and provides evidence for the BSD conjecture. 

To arrive at these outcomes, we employ an approach based on sieve inequalities, specifically the Birch and Recillas inequality, in combination with the application of Galois cohomology. We extend the use of these techniques to a broader context, making our findings applicable to all quartic extensions with Galois groups $S_4$ and $A_4$. Furthermore, we develop a new approach to evaluating the rank of elliptic curves through the calculation of local data, facilitated by the application of Galois cohomology. 

Finally, we note that our findings on rank growth have implications for the study of Diophantine equations with genus 2 curves as variables. Consequently, we establish a new approach to solving certain types of these equations, namely those of the form $E(n) = O$, where $E$ is an elliptic curve and $n$ is an integer. This method enables the determination of all integer solutions to this type of equation within a specific range. By sharing common factors, SSCNF can utilize a minimal amount of supervised information to produce a more accurate and musically coherent representation of the data. This formulation differs significantly from the conventional Carter-Lichnerowicz approach, allowing us to directly solve the complex Einstein field equations through the use of a conjugate gradient method, without requiring the derivation of semi-analytical equations. Our method is particularly well-suited for complex configurations, such as those involving massive rotating stars with neutron star companions, and we highlight the advantages of our approach over traditional methods, including a greater sensitivity to perturbations and a more efficient convergence, resulting in more accurate results with less computational demands. The growing interest in emotional knowledge and related tasks such as sentiment analysis and emotional text classification highlights the importance of high-quality annotated datasets. However, manually annotating texts with emotions is a labor-intensive process, and human evaluators may make errors due to the complexity and subjectivity of emotional judgments. As a result, it is essential to develop methods to efficiently and effectively revise and refine existing annotations, particularly for texts that are only partially or incorrectly labeled. In this study, we introduce a BERT-based approach, called RevisionAnnotator, which leverages pre-trained natural language processing models, specifically BERT, to suggest alternative emotion labels for given texts. We evaluate our method on an existing dataset and achieve notable results, notably including the finding that human evaluators tend to agree with the suggested labels more often than the original annotations given the context of the texts. Furthermore, we observe human evaluators' agreement with each other but not with the initially provided annotations. As a secondary goal, we also explore the potential of our approach to inform the refinement of existing datasets, a task we term RevisionAnnotating. Along with presenting our method and associated experiments, we too contribute a new RevisionAnnotating dataset, which we make publicly available to the research community. This new dataset, unlike traditional annotation datasets, includes texts with already assigned emotion labels, in addition to the actual text content. Consequently, it offers a more comprehensive data set suitable for various natural language processing tasks, such as text classification, in comparison to text content alone. This new aspect enables the evaluation of the effectiveness of our RevisionAnnotator method, which aims to determine whether the suggested labels align with the pre-assigned emotion labels. Our experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, and we anticipate that it will serve as a valuable resource for researchers working on the refinement of existing annotated datasets. This approach and associated data sets are relevant to the field of affective computing and may be applicable to other domains that rely on the use of pre-trained language models, such as legal text classification and medical text analysis. Additionally, our RevisionAnnotator method may be useful for enhancing the performance of deep learning-based emotion classification models, and we plan to explore this possibility in our ongoing research. In 1991, Herman and Plotkin introduced the concept of normalization by evaluation (NBE) for typed lambda calculi, providing a semantic basis for analyzing the normalization properties of type theories. This technique has been the focus of recent research on the lambda cube, with multiple authors developing NBE proofs for various type theories. This dissertation explores the application of robust normalization, a refinement of NBE, to the calculus of constructions (CoC), a widely used type theory. Originally, the correctness of robust normalization proofs relied on the coherence of the context; however, this dissertation demonstrates how to modify robust normalization to account for the incompleteness of the context, thereby ensuring the validity of the normalization result for the calculus of constructions. Additionally, this work is being incorporated into the Homotopy Type Theory (HoTT) library, with the goal of affirming the correctness of the computational beta and eta equality proofs, as required for the HoTT foundation. Furthermore, this dissertation investigates the use of the refined robust normalization to prove the termination of the CoC typed gobini calculus, an extension of the gobini language with typing. Originally, the correctness of the termination proof relied on the context-to-term property; however, this property is insufficient due to the incompleteness of the context, resulting in the need for an alternative demonstration of termination. Finally, this research is being conducted in the presence of dependent types and the sigma (product) type, with the inclusion of a dependent termination proof for the CoC typed gobini calculus. The techniques developed in this research are also applicable to the extension of the lambda cube with dependent types. The name "robust normalization" was proposed by Herman, and the term is being adopted in this dissertation; however, Herman personally communicates that he would have preferred the name "efficient normalization". As a mark of respect for Herman's preference, the name "efficient normalization" will be used in the HoTT library. Nonetheless, the name "robust normalization" will continue to be employed in this dissertation. Additionally, this research is being conducted under the supervision of Paul L. T. H. B. Concurrent object-oriented programming is widely adopted in various industries due to its clear and effective code expression, thereby being a fundamental skill for concurrent programming to be taught in university computer science courses.  However, a significant challenge in teaching this skill is creating a suitable reference framework, especially for educational purposes on GPU systems.  Existing frameworks either focus on demonstrating high performance or illustrating good programming practices, but they do not simultaneously achieve both goals.

Our research involves developing a concurrent object-oriented reference framework called DynaSOAr, specifically designed for educational GPU programming.  This framework provides an excellent balance of high performance, clear code, and simple object allocation, making it an ideal teaching tool for concurrent object-oriented programming on GPU systems.  By using DynaSOAr as a reference, students can gain a deeper understanding of concurrent object allocation and memory access, two crucial skills in programming for modern parallel computing systems.  We also conduct a clear and detailed analysis of the memory access patterns of DynaSOAr, and the performance of up to 256 GPUs is thoroughly evaluated, showing that DynaSOAr can achieve over 90% of the theoretical maximum performance while maintaining a slow memory access speed of around 30 GBps.  Furthermore, case studies and surveys have validated the educational effectiveness of DynaSOAr from both the instructor's and the student's perspectives.  The source code of DynaSOAr has been publicly released on GitHub, providing a reliable reference framework for concurrent object-oriented programming on GPU systems for both industrial practitioners and the academic community.  By using DynaSOAr as an example, we have developed a clear and concise tutorial on concurrent object allocation and memory access, demonstrating how to integrate DynaSOAr with user applications while maximizing performance.  This reference framework can be integrated with popular GPU programming frameworks such as CUDA-IO and CUDA-ML, and is compatible with a wide range of GPU devices, including data centers and desktop computers equipped with NVIDIA GPUs from the K20 to the A100 series.  In addition, DynaSOAr can also be easily adapted for programming other types of parallel hardware systems that support concurrent object allocation and memory access.  We believe that DynaSOAr will become a valuable resource for teaching concurrent object-oriented programming on GPU systems, and with its high performance, clear code, and simple memory allocation, it will benefit both industrial practitioners and the academic community.  Additionally, DynaSOAr can also be used as a demonstration example for showcasing the performance benefits of concurrent object-oriented programming on GPU systems.

This proposed "self-induced translucency" ion thruster is expected to achieve beam velocities in excess of 300,000 kilometers per second, enabling the development of advanced interstellar propulsion systems. The theoretical model is used to design a simple positron recapture device consisting of a pair of parallel plates, and both analytical and computational simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this design in enhancing the velocity of a beam of ions. A basic ion thruster design incorporating a self-induced translucency field is also proposed and computations are performed to analyze its performance. We examined the electronic and magnetic configurations of carbon and nitrogen impurities in titanium dioxide.  We found that a substitutional carbon dopant forms a bond with an oxygen atom, takes on a double positive charge, and exhibits spin polarization.  In contrast, a nitrogen dopant that forms a triple positive charge with no spin polarization was found in a interstitial position.  A negative charge on a nearby oxygen atom is present in both scenarios.  Calculated optical characteristics suggest these arrangements could be observable with experimental techniques like EPR and ENDOR.  Models of a carbon dopant with oxygen suggest a positive charge on the oxygen atom may lead to luminescence around 3.1 eV.  In contrast, a nitrogen dopant with no spin polarization may not exhibit this type of luminescence.  This research could be applied to improving solar energy technologies by increasing the lifespan of TiO$_2$ photocatalysts.  Both carbon and nitrogen dopants may also be useful in developing magnetic TiO$_2$ materials with minimal impact on their photocatalytic properties.  This could be especially useful in preventing the degradation of photocatalysts during magnetic field treatments.  A comparison of our results to earlier studies is also presented in this report.  Earlier research on carbon and nitrogen dopants in TiO$_2$ often relied on semi-empirical methods that may not accurately account for magnetic polarization.  Our results also provide a explanation for the limited success of experiments aimed at developing magnetic TiO$_2$ by focusing on the need for a more precise understanding of the arrangement of these dopants within this material. Furthermore, discovering this process would not only shed light on the origin of the top quark mass but also offer a novel probe of the Higgs sector and a new avenue for top quark production studies. Moreover, if found at a rate of $\sigma \sim 1$ fb, this process would also provide a new origin for a substantial fraction of the observed top quark production in hadron colliders. Using numerical simulations, our previous research demonstrated the existence of scale-dependent biases in temperature measurements, which can impact structure function estimates. The current study builds upon this work by examining how measurement inaccuracies influence the determination of structure functions, specifically focusing on the following aspects: the identification of inertial ranges, slope measurements, and the distribution of cluster temperatures. A theoretical model measuring temperature uncertainties has been developed and utilized in the analysis. Our research reveals that temperature inaccuracies can lead to the misidentification of inertial ranges and biased slope calculations in structure functions. Furthermore, the distribution of temperature uncertainties follows a bi-modal pattern, indicating a distinction between gas at the center of clusters and peripheral gas. Our findings imply that temperature inaccuracies can result in scale-dependent biases in slope calculations, which can be understood through the lens of a theoretical model. Located at the heart of the Milky Way lies the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ), a distinct ring structure composed of dense molecular gas. Recent observations suggest that the mass configuration within this ring is aligned with the plane defined by the line of sight, the normal to the plane, and the major axis of the ring. To verify and quantify this anisotropy, we employed a two-dimensional correlation function method to analyze publicly available velocity-channel maps of the $^{12}$CO (1-0) emission from the CMZ. By calculating the second moment of velocity dispersion along specific axes, we determined the anisotropy of the velocity dispersion to be $1.24\pm0.05$, which indicates a moderate level of alignment. We also explored other indicators, including the velocity gradient, shear rate, and radial profile of velocity dispersion, and found them to be insensitive to anisotropy. However, our results suggest that the anisotropy of velocity dispersion may vary along different radial segments of the CMZ. To interpret these findings, we considered several factors including stellar shear, bar potential, and the presence of small-scale density fluctuations. Our research highlights the capability of the two-dimensional correlation function method in analyzing complex anisotropic configurations and suggests that further studies are needed to fully understand the physics governing gas behavior within the CMZ. Moreover, we propose using this technique to investigate other molecular gas structures found in the nuclei of nearby galaxies. By employing high-fidelity observations and modeling the effects of gas dynamics, future studies will be capable of extracting more subtle anisotropies and identifying potential patterns related to galaxy morphology and other features. Additionally, the two-dimensional correlation function method can be utilized to design optimized surveys for detecting anisotropic gas structures, thus paving the way for a more comprehensive exploration of the multifaceted physics governing the behavior of gas in the nuclei of galaxies. This approach was tested on a large dataset of facial video recordings and produced accurate results. This research develops a tiny temperature detection system with a precision of 0.24°C, capable of functioning between 0.6V and 1.8V, and is designed for energy harvesting applications where the operating voltage may fluctuate due to changing environmental temperature. The proposed detector is a binary search-based system that employs two sub-threshold MOSFETs as sensitive elements, leverages dynamic threshold voltage variation for increased sensitivity, and is powered by weak bias currents generated from a diode-connected transistor. The system's effectiveness was verified through the fabrication of a test chip using a 180nm CMOS process, demonstrating a detection capability between 0.6V and 1.8V with a resolution of 0.24°C, an error of ±1.4°C, and an energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion. Moreover, the designed detector demonstrates the feasibility of incorporating it into a temperature feedback control system. Experimental evaluations of the system's performance under varying supply voltages are also conducted, showcasing the detector's ability to provide accurate temperature readings even in the sub-volt region. The study also involves the analysis of a practical application scenario using the designed detector in a phase change memory-based self-adaptive loop, and the results indicate the detector's effectiveness in achieving optimal energy consumption and retaining data under different supply voltage conditions. The study is further supported by the availability of a test chip with a area of 0.25mm² and a bandwidth of 10kHz. The study is co-advised by Prof. Dejan Vukovic and Prof. Sungtae Kwon. Music theory education often employs a question-and-answer approach between a student and an expert music theorist. Leveraging artificial intelligence in this context can be challenging because existing models are designed to process linear sequences of information but may not account for the complex, cyclic nature of musical concepts. Our proposed model, called Pied Piper, uses a unique cyclic reasoning mechanism inspired by multi-hop attention models. In an evaluation of Pied Piper against other language model variants, it showed a notable improvement in retaining musical theory information over time. Additionally, Pied Piper was found to effectively incorporate diverse sources of background knowledge when answering questions about music theory. Human assessors confirmed these findings in a separate, more in-depth evaluation of the model's performance. Our analysis of the model's results suggests that Pied Piper excels at answering questions by identifying key concepts in music theory. As a strong candidate for applications in music theory education, such as providing personalized lessons, we publicly release Pied Piper pre-trained on a vast music theory corpus. Furthermore, we explore the potential of meta-questionable instances, which can guide the model in exploring new topics or refining its existing knowledge. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in identifying novel musical concepts with ease. With its unique ability to tackle complex, cyclic subject matters, Pied Piper may also be a suitable model for other domains characterized by cyclic structures, such as graph theory and gene regulation. A massive infrared dark cloud, dubbed the Dragon, has been analyzed at 1.3 mm and 850 $\mu$m using the SHARC2 and SCOPE submm cameras on the APEX telescope, and at 1.1 mm and 850 $\mu$m using the HOBYS2 and SCOPE on the APEX telescope. This study explores extensions of classical modal logic centered on prelinearity, specifically considering duality-based and relational semantics. We examine algebraic and relational frameworks for Godel modal logic and its extensions with intuitionistic and classical modal operators. These examinations apply to modal logics derived from prelinearity, including their treatment of distributivity and the addition of modal operators with opposite intensions. This research also investigates the underlying algebras and relational structures of bisimulation, demonstrating their distributivity and the behavior of modal operators under the application of prelinearity. Finally, we explore the addition of modal operators with opposite intensions in these algebras and structures. This study specifically delves into Sahlqvist correspondence for these modal logics within the context of canonical extension. LiDAR technology equips vehicles with a valuable set of 3D point cloud data, enabling them to detect surroundings and navigate through various environments.  For automated decision-making, these points are often used in conjunction with other sensory data, such as radar and camera input.  In the field of machine learning, processing raw 3D point cloud data directly can be complicated, so it's often pre-processed into more manageable forms, such as intensity images or 2D occupancy grids.  However, losing dimensioned data during this conversion process may impair the performance of subsequent classification algorithms.  This paper evaluates the capabilities of machine learning models when trained on raw 3D point cloud data, spanning various scenarios including urban environments, comparing their accuracy to that of models trained on derived sensory data, such as intensity images and occupancy grids.  The results show that deep learning models can achieve superior classification performance when working directly with raw 3D point cloud data.  The study further assesses the impact of various LiDAR settings on classification performance, examining how changing the frequency and field of view affects the detection of key objects, including discovering that increased scanning frequency and field of view leads to more accurate classifications.  The findings imply that high-quality LiDAR data, combined with appropriate machine learning algorithms, can deliver superior performance, outperforming more complex and costly 3D sensor configurations.  The research is conducted through a customized evaluation platform, comprising a tailored dataset and evaluation protocol, which is made available to the community to guide future research in this area.  The study's results suggest that future research focus on developing more efficient and versatile deep learning architectures, capable of handling a wide range of LiDAR configurations and applications.  The work is a collaboration between NVIDIA and ZF, a leading autonomous vehicle technology supplier.  The evaluation platform and associated data are being developed in conjunction with the company's efforts to drive advancements in LiDAR-based machine learning.  The research is being presented at the 2019 IEEE Intelligent Transportation Systems Conference.  A accompanying video illustrating the evaluation platform and results can be found at the conference's associated website.  The team behind this research also invites participants to join the competition for developing top-performing machine learning models, as well as the challenge of enhancing the evaluation platform and related datasets.  Those interested in contributing should reach out to the authors directly.  The evaluation platform and associated datasets can be found at the provided URL.  This research is an effort to drive innovation in LiDAR-based machine learning

Recent observations suggest that neutrinos, ultra-high-energy cosmic gamma-rays, and cosmic rays may originate from the same sources. However, the sources of these particles are not yet fully identified. To better understand the possible connections among these particles, we need to analyze their spatial relationships with each other. Considering the limitations and systematic uncertainties of current datasets, we need to be cautious when searching for correlations spatially. In this study, we propose a rigorous statistical test to identify the presence of spatial correlations among neutrinos, ultra-high-energy cosmic gamma-rays, and cosmic rays on various scales, ranging from 1 degree to 5 degrees. We apply our test to publicly available datasets of neutrinos and cosmic gamma-rays from the IceCube neutrino telescope and find evidence of spatial correlations between neutrinos and cosmic gamma-rays at a 2 degrees scale. Additionally, we discover that the sources of neutrinos and cosmic gamma-rays are separated into two distinct regions on the celestial sky, consistent with the distribution of cosmic rays as inferred from cosmic gamma-rays. Our analysis also reveals that about 6% of the sky contains at least one source of neutrinos and cosmic gamma-rays, while the density of these sources is approximately 0.84±0.20 (stat.) ± 0.16 (syst.) per steradian. Furthermore, we find that the spatial distribution of neutrinos and cosmic gamma-rays is significantly different from a random arrangement at a 4% confidence level. Our analysis provides new insights into the spatial relationships among neutrinos, ultra-high-energy cosmic gamma-rays, and cosmic rays, offering a framework for further research in this field. This research can be adapted to analyze future datasets from more sensitive and powerful neutrino detectors and cosmic gamma-ray observatories. This study can also be applied to identify the sources of multi-TeV cosmic gamma-rays and neutrinos, such as the sources surrounding the binary black hole and neutron star merger event GW170817. This research can be used to predict the distribution of cosmic neutrinos and gamma-rays on the celestial sky, such as the distribution of neutrinos around high-energy cosmic gamma-ray sources such as TXS 0506+056 and the pulsar PSR B1706+44. This study can be adapted to search for spatial correlations between cosmic neutrinos and gamma-rays and other types of cosmic messengers, such as high-energy cosmic rays, gravitational waves, supernovae explosions, and the distribution of cosmic baryons. The complex interplay between a liquid's surface tension and the roughness of the surfaces it comes into contact with determines the friction it experiences when moving over another liquid of the same type. While this interplay has been extensively studied for smooth surfaces, little is known about how rough surfaces made of texturized materials affect a liquid's viscosity. In this study, researchers created a type of surface made up of hexagonal patterns of liquid film and used it to show that the viscosity of a liquid film is significantly affected by these texturized surfaces, especially when compared to smooth surfaces. Additionally, they found that this increase in viscosity holds true even at very small particle sizes, at which point it is driven by the disorder created in the liquid's film structure rather than any roughness present. Moreover, this phenomenon was observed not just in soap solutions but also in oil and water mixtures, and it could have implications for how liquids move over other rough surfaces, especially those made of texturized materials, which are ubiquitous in nature and are used in many applications. In order to model this phenomenon, researchers developed a theory that takes into account the disorder created in the liquid's film structure rather than any roughness present, and it was supported by computer simulations of the behavior of the liquid film. In contrast to other types of disorder, such as the kind created by shaking, this type of surface has the unique ability to induce long-lasting disorder in the liquids that come into contact with it, and it does this through a mechanism called capillary elasto-dynamics that gives rise to the complex patterns that form in the liquid when it is placed on the surface. Understanding this phenomenon could also help scientists to learn more about the behavior of liquids in other complex environments, such as those with defects, and it could have implications for how liquids move over other rough surfaces, especially those made of texturized materials, which are ubiquitous in nature and are used in many applications. This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on classifying skin carcinomas using histological images, and developed a method for detecting anomalous images used in training. A classification model was created by establishing a threshold for rejecting images deemed not carcinomas, and then combining their features to enhance the detection of carcinomas. For the challenge, this approach yielded a precision of 54.27% on the test dataset. Additionally, we discovered our techniques may be applied to identifying outlier samples, and explored this by identifying features that distinguish normal skin from carcinomas, and flagging images with features more akin to the latter as potential outliers. This strategy achieved a precision of 73.19% on the challenge's validation dataset. All experiments were conducted using Python with the Keras and OpenCV libraries.

The intricate patterns formed by viscous fluids when they invade their neighbors, also known as Saffman--Breuel--Proudman modes, are a remarkable display of the complex dynamics produced by interactions between rotation, surface tension, and buoyancy. In a study using a Hele-Shaw cell, researchers extend the scope of these modes by creating an environment where the surrounding air is displaced with a non-buoyant fluid, such as oil. This setup enables them to explore modes involving multiple fingers in both stationary and rotating cells, including a novel, asymmetric mode found in the latter. A theoretical analysis of this mode predicts its instability and capacity for bending, supported by findings from both the Hele-Shaw cell and a related experiment using a layer of fluid within a circular container. These discoveries provide a basis for further investigation into the wide range of finger configurations that can develop in the Hele-Shaw cell, including those with up to six distinct branches. In addition, this study introduces a new scale that determines the width of each mode and identifies key conditions under which some modes become unstable, resulting in the bending or bending-and-twisting of adjacent fingers. These discoveries are expected to contribute to a deeper understanding of the complex interactions that produce a variety of finger configurations in both two and three-dimensional systems. Additionally, this study reveals similarities between the finger patterns produced by the Hele-Shaw cell and a related system involving a layer of fluid within a circular container, such as a layer of oil surrounded by air in a cylinder. This similarity holds promise for further exploring the behavior of these patterns with different types of fluids in both stationary and rotating cells. Furthermore, this study provides a basis for investigating other two-dimensional systems that exhibit similar behavior and that are now known to be governed by the same rules that apply to the Hele-Shaw cell. In addition, this study also introduces new challenges for the development of interface fluids that are used in experiments and could potentially be developed with the ability to change their properties in response to changes in the rotation rate of a cell. In the context of the Hele-Shaw cell, this would require the ability to alter the viscosity and surface tension of the interface fluids independently. This study demonstrates that even small changes in the properties of these fluids can result in significant changes in the behavior of the modes and could potentially be used to create new types of patterns with different numbers of branches by carefully selecting the properties of the fluids used in a cell. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One such strategy involves the careful planning of learning environments that are tailored to elicit different types of curiosity.  As learning environments are increasingly shifting online, it is essential to develop a more comprehensive understanding of how to design these environments to stimulate curiosity in an e-learning setting.  One such approach is known as the Learning Science Strategy, which is focused on identifying the underlying scientific principles that govern how people learn.  However, there is a lack of empirical research on the application of this approach, particularly in an e-learning environment.  One such research project is described in this study, where college students worked in small groups on an online learning platform to complete a programming course.  The research team developed a comprehensive measure of curiosity that is composed of three distinct components, including interest, exploration, and uncertainty.  The effectiveness of the Learning Science Strategy was evaluated using a within-subjects design, where each student served as their own control.  The results showed a statistically significant increase in curiosity over time, as well as significant differences in the levels of curiosity exhibited by each student.  The research team analyzed the data from multiple perspectives, including the overall group, individual males, individual females, as well as the distribution of curiosity levels.  The findings indicate that the Learning Science Strategy is effective in stimulating curiosity in college students in an e-learning environment.  The data also provide valuable insights into the dynamics of curiosity in this setting, including the presence of individual differences, as well as gender-based variations.  The research team is exploring ways to adapt this approach for use in educational settings that focus on detecting and stimulating curiosity in real-time.  One such approach involves the development of an automated tool that can identify students who are exhibiting high levels of curiosity, as well as those who are displaying low levels of curiosity.  This tool can alert the instructor to intervene and provide additional support to students who are struggling, as well as recognize and reward students who are exhibiting high levels of curiosity.  This approach has the potential to enhance the effectiveness of learning science strategies in stimulating curiosity in an e-learning environment, as well as in educational settings that detect and stimulate curiosity

The creation of efficient and eco-friendly urban road networks depends on the optimal selection of roads for detection, making it essential to identify and monitor road conditions. This paper utilizes a stochastic geometric approach to develop a method for detecting all roads in an urban area on a given day, based on the optimal placement of sensors on vehicles, and proves the existence of an optimal non-degenerate solution. This optimal solution is then approximated using a non-degenerate configuration that minimizes the number of roads missed. A computational model and simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in detecting roads under various conditions. While machine learning-based nucleus segmentation holds great promise for clinical applications, extracting accurate annotations from experts is a significant challenge due to the complex nature of cell nuclei. This paper introduces a novel two-stage network, W-Net, specifically designed for robust nucleus identification in histopathology images. The first stage, a nucleus-supervision network, is trained to identify and mark difficult-to-differentiate nucleus regions using a smaller dataset. A second stage, a closed-region network, is then trained on the complete dataset with constraints, using the marked regions to prioritize focus on nucleus identification within those areas. Systematic experiments demonstrate W-Net's effectiveness, showcasing superior performance compared to state-of-the-art segmentation models. Implementation details and comprehensive evaluation results are provided, highlighting the potential applications and future directions for this approach. Source code is available online at https://github.com/zwang84/WS-Network.

We introduce a new, flexible representation for algorithmic correctness proofs, ensuring that an implementation accurately executes a specified program. This new framework, called rational pseudocode, bridges the gap between traditional algorithm descriptions and their modern, interactive code representations. To demonstrate the utility of rational pseudocode, we apply it to create formal proofs of correctness for two popular algorithms: Dijkstra's shortest path and Karger's minimum cut. Our approach uses the Agda programming language to define both the pseudocode and the proofs of correctness. We also investigate the benefits of this approach, recognizing that it shares common goals with the Rational Programmers Project. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions to our method and consider how irrational code, corresponding to faulty implementations, could be incorporated into our framework. As a result, a developer could define an irrational code variant for a given algorithm and automatically generate a corresponding rational code version with accompanying proofs of correctness. This could significantly streamline the algorithm implementation process, making it more efficient and error-free. Finally, we reflect on the experience of using rational pseudocode and identify areas for further research in this area. With the rise of interactive proof assistants and semi-automated code generation tools, our approach may also be of interest to the broader programming languages community. In particular, we believe that our method could be used to create novel educational course materials that combine code examples with formal proofs of correctness, thus providing an engaging and effective way to teach fundamental algorithms concepts. In addition, we discuss how our approach could be applied to develop new forms of educational content, such as (1) instructional videos featuring interactive code examples accompanied by formal proofs, and (2) hands-on, algorithm-focused workshops that combine code implementations with formal proofs of correctness. These educational concepts, inspired by our use of rational pseudocode, are currently being explored as potential new courses at the University of Edinburgh's Informatics Teaching Laboratory. With the growing availability of interactive code tools and proof assistants, our approach is now more feasible than ever, and we anticipate that it will become an increasingly popular method for creating novel educational content. In fact, we are already seeing evidence of this trend, as reflected in the rising number of code proof-of-concept submissions to programming language workshops and conferences. As a result, we believe that our method is well-positioned to make a significant impact in this area. In conclusion, our experience with rational pseudocode has shown that it is an effective way to create novel code proof-of-concepts that combine implementation with formal proofs of correctness. In the context of information retrieval, where we have a dataset of $n$ multidimensional points, we want to maintain a dynamic clustering of at most $k$ points for information purposes. As new points are added or old points are removed, the clustering needs to adapt to ensure that the distance between any two grouped points is greater than a set threshold $\delta$. The goal is to design an efficient algorithm that creates and updates clusters under this condition with minimal computational expense, specifically sublinear time. Our research focuses on identifying the most stringent requirements for $\delta$ that allows such an algorithm to exist and function effectively. Our findings show that, without utilizing any external memory, there is an existential threshold of $\delta = \sqrt{\log n/\dim}$ for $k=2$, and a lower bound of $\delta = \sqrt{\log n/d}\cdot \sqrt{\log \log n}$ for $k=3$. Moreover, we present an efficient algorithm that meets these requirements and performs at least $k$ iterations of a specific dynamic $k$-means process. Our work also highlights the importance of compact clustering in data presentation. Additionally, we provide an algorithm with near-optimal performance for the standard dynamic $k$-means problem in $d$-dimensional space with small distortion. Our method is applicable to any $p$-mean with $2\le p\le \infty$. Our results are based on a novel connection between dynamic clustering and semi-randomized online learning. We introduce a hierarchical framework for analyzing multi-agent competitive situations with random movements in bounded areas. The beauty of our approach lies in its simplicity - we've developed a method for calculating the overall success probability of one agent (the pursuer) in capturing another (the evader) in a given environment. This method is so straightforward that it allows us to create visual representations of the pursuer's chances of success in various scenarios. Furthermore, our approach can be applied to more complex environments by breaking them down into simpler sub-regions, effectively utilizing the underlying symmetry in a meaningful way. This hierarchy of analysis becomes particularly valuable when the motion probabilities are equal, as it leads to a very intuitive and easily graspable understanding of the evader's success probabilities in each sub-region. This approach to analysis also extends to scenarios with more than two agents in a fair manner, as it considers the overall 'team' success probability in an collaborative context, where the agents are cooperative rather than competitive. This insight is then combined with the concept of sub-region 'difficulty levels', leading to a visual representation of the success probabilities of the evader in scenarios with an unfair game. This approach has been numerically validated using Monte Carlo simulations and has been applied to simple 3D environments with varying levels of complexity as well as some complex 2D environments with multiple rooms. In solving inverse problems in imaging, the degree of smoothing is a key issue. While strong smoothing loses important detail and weak smoothing is prone to noise, finding the optimal balance is challenging. This research presents a novel approach, centered on a regularized conditional Generative Adversarial Network (cgan), to automatically extract the unique solution component from given data. This method enhances previous GAN-based solutions by incorporating two crucial elements: a conditionally constrained loss function and extra regularization. In numerical experiments using the inverse source problem formulation for the Helmholtz equation, our approach demonstrates superior performance in comparison to standard GAN-based solutions and other regularization techniques. Furthermore, this research is not limited to imaging inverse problems but is also applicable to other inverse problems involving parameter identification. Additionally, we derive a theoretical stability bound for our cgan method. Overall, our results suggest that this approach is an effective and efficient way to solve inverse problems. Finally, this research is accompanied by easily implementable MATLAB codes for numerical experiments. Next-generation wireless networks face significant challenges due to high frequency THz communications, which can lead to spotty channel estimation and degraded performance. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through dilated convolution neural networks (DCNNs). WN's success in generating high-fidelity audio can be attributed to its capability to produce detailed waveform representations. However, WN's pitch control is restricted to the duration of a single analysis window. To overcome this limitation and capture semi-periodic sound patterns, QPNet embeds additional features within its DCNNs using dilated convolution layers, enabling the model to produce high-fidelity audio with sustained semi- periodic components and other non-stationary sound patterns. Experimental evaluations using the LJSpeech dataset demonstrate QPNet's effectiveness in generating high-quality, semi-periodic audio with reduced pitch dependence and marginal increases in computational costs. Comparative assessments with WN and a pitch-sensitive DCNN-based precursor (PSDCNN) confirm QPNet's superior performance in generating audio with semi-periodic patterns. The proposed architecture's effectiveness is further validated through perceptual evaluation and a complementary analysis of PSDCNN. The implementation of a quasi-periodic autoregressive raw waveform generative model based on QPNet is also introduced and found to achieve state-of-the-art performance in speech synthesis. The model's potential applications in musical sound design are also explored. Our primary acoustic cue for localizing sound is based on inter-aural differences in arrival times and sound pressure levels between the two ears, which are severely limited in their range by the human head.  These constraints result in relatively small differences in time and level, which are often comparable to the natural variability present in a person's auditory system.  To compensate for this, nature has developed a stereophonic sound with numerous cues, consisting of a diverse range of natural sounds.  However, even though we're able to accurately localize sounds recorded in a quiet forest, we struggle to do so with sounds recorded in heavy traffic.  This difficulty has inspired researchers to create artificial speech enhancement methods, but these techniques often degrade the localizing ability of natural sounds within recorded speech.  This paper discusses a novel approach that focuses on preserving the head-related transfer function, and achieves notable success in localizing speech recorded under various conditions, even when compared to cutting-edge methods like DNN-based techniques.  This approach is complemented by an explanatory model, which highlights the underlying challenges and identifies key factors that contribute to localizing artificial sounds but not natural ones within recorded speech.  This model sparks the idea to apply this approach to speech enhancement methods and expect it to yield better performance.  To verify this, we create a new synthesis framework that integrates our method with a typical speech enhancement method, and the results validate our hypothesis by delivering even better performance.  This new framework allows us to accurately localize sounds within recorded speech, a challenging task even for the human auditory system.  This paper presents the novel approach, the model, and the new synthesis framework, which represents a first step in addressing this complex issue.  However, it's essential to acknowledge that localizing sounds within recorded speech is an intricate problem, and our solution might not be comprehensive, which is why we invite the research community to build upon this work. We derive concise formulas for diagonalizing the Hamiltonians and secondary conserved operators, and we identify the eigenvalues as functions of the Bethe ansatz roots. These results are applicable to any higher-spin XXZ chain where the 'leg' spins are identical. Furthermore, we establish a direct connection between the XXZ chain and the algebraic Bethe ansatz, without requiring a pseudo-spin chain transformation. This enables us to define the symmetry-algebra structure explicitly, making it clear that the XXZ chain itself constitutes an affine quantum-algebra representation. This perspective allows us to identify the spin values for the XXZ chain's highest-weight state, providing a derivation for the form factors and correlation functions directly from the algebra, without referring to the string hypothesis. This involves using the naked root system, without any 'clothing' provided by the string. Consequently, any form factor can be viewed as a representation of the algebra, given a given set of discrete Bethe ansatz roots. Speech translation combines speech recognition and machine translation to enable language interpretation. This would allow people to listen to a translation of spoken language, rather than reading it. This paper explores the challenge of training a single model to perform this task across multiple language pairs, rather than optimizing for each pair individually. Our proposed approach, known as zero-shot speech translation, leverages a shared multimodal encoder and decoder structure to facilitate the translation of spoken language into any target language, without prior training on that language pair. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to 10 language pairs, using data available on parallel text corpora and large datasets of unpaired speech transcripts. Our evaluation reveals that a zero-shot speech translator can achieve a similar quality of translation as a model trained on parallel speech data, for most language pairs tested. We also examine the factors that influence this challenge, including the size of available training data and the similarity between source and target languages. We release our models and implementation details in an open-source repository, to facilitate further research in this area.
